newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU monetary committee to meet on single currency.
newsitem.headline: EU monetary committee to meet on single currency.

text.p: The European Union's monetary committee, an important behind-the-scenes player in Europe's drive towards a single currency, will meet on Monday to discuss a budget stability pact, sources said on Friday.
The group, comprising national treasury and central bank officials, will also focus energies on a new Exchange Rate Mechanism that links countries inside a monetary union to those on the perimeter.
Legal issues pertaining to single currency will be the final item on the agenda, with the members expected to gather on Tuesday as well, sources added.
"I would be surprised to see a solution to the stability pact next week," said one monetary source.

EU monetary officials believe that a stability pact designed to enforce budgetary discipline among countries inside economic and monetary union (EMU) will be the hardest challenge among the three items up for discussion.
"I think we will get a mandate to work out a solution by December," said another source. "That will be important from the German perspective."

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, the primary catalyst behind a budget stability pact, has argued that sanctions on countries running excessive deficits should be automatic -- a term that has left many groping for a more precise definition.

Monetary officials say the problem so far is how to agree on a formula that makes the EU's current excessive deficits procedure more swift and punitive. But there are limits to how far they can go given the strictures of the Maastricht treaty.
"I think the big hurdle is this automaticity thing," added the source.

While there is agreement that countries running persistent deficits -- above three percent of total output -- should be penalised, the "presumption" that sanctions will be enforced is still considered ill-defined.
As one official put it: "One has to wonder what the presumption of sanctions really means."
On Thursday, EU monetary affairs commissioner Yves-Thibault de Silguy said he was optimistic that an accord could be reached but added that several issues needed to be resolved.

One concerns the period from when a country is deemed to have an excessive deficit to when it must put forward a plan to rectify it. De Silguy said the shortest possible time frame would be nine months, with most countries divided over whether it could be as long as 12 months.
For example, the decision on whether a government had an excessive deficit would be made in March of the following year once reliable data is available.
The offending government would then have until December to put forward a plan to bring its finances under control. If the plan was considered not credible the government could be fined.
German officials have argued for a shorter period of six to seven months.
The decisions reached next week will be forwarded to an informal meeting of EU finance ministers and central bankers in Dublin on September 21.
